title: Artificial intelligence and elections
summary:
As artificial intelligence has become more mainstream, there is growing concern about how this will influence elections. Potential targets of AI include election processes, election offices, election officials and election vendors. Generative AI capabilities allow creation of misleading content, including text-to-video, deepfake videos, text-to-image, AI-altered images, text-to-speech, voice cloning, and text-to-text. In the context of an election, a deepfake video of a candidate may propagate information that the candidate does not endorse. Chatbots could spread misinformation related to election locations, times or voting methods. In contrast to malicious actors in the past, these techniques require little technical skill and can spread rapidly.

Notable examples from 2024 elections include Indonesia, where Prabowo Subianto made extensive use of AI-generated art in his campaign; South Korea, where deepfakes were used to spread misinformation with 129 deepfake violations of election laws within a two-week period; Taiwan, where AI-generated content included a deepfake video of Xi Jinping; the United Kingdom, where AI-generated videos spread on social media including a deepfake of PM Rishi Sunak; and the United States, where officials from the ODNI and FBI stated that Russia, Iran, and China used generative AI tools to create fake and divisive content.

The use of artificial intelligence was described as an accelerant rather than a revolutionary change to influence efforts. LLM-generated messages have the capacity to persuade humans on political issues. Authorities worldwide are trying to establish guardrails, with efforts including banning AI-generated voices in robocalls in the U.S., major tech companies signing a pact to prevent AI from disrupting elections, and the EU's AI Act imposing obligations for transparency, detection, and tracing of AI-generated material.
